[quote=vespurias;60248153][spoiler= [b][nation]The Crystalline Empire[/nation] & [nation]Vespurias[/nation] : [i]The Empire of Elseyr-Vespurias[/i][/b]]

[b]PETTY IMPERIAL POLITICS[/b]

[b]Imperial Steward Election[/b]

The first Imperial Steward of Vespurias was elected in a blaze of compromise. Not the sort of blaze that burned brightly, nor even one that warmed the room; more the weary flicker of a candle left too close to the window, sputtering because no one could quite decide where to put it.

James George Hacker, Baron Hacker of Islington, KG, PC, BSc (Ksmt.), Hon. D.Phil. (Avrn.), had been many things: a Minister for Administrative Affairs in High Albany, a party loyalist, a committee-filler, a safe pair of hands. In short, a man who could offend no one except those who demanded vision. He was the candidate the factions could tolerate, which is to say he was the candidate no one really wanted but everyone eventually settled on.

The Civil Service had smiled politely, adjusted their spectacles, and quietly arranged matters so that Hackers "surprise" victory was anything but. Ballots were cast, results tallied, and the announcement made with due ceremony. Hacker himself appeared both delighted and horrified, as though he had been chosen to judge a school raffle only to discover the prize was running an empire.

Me? Steward? Oh, well, yes, I suppose I can steward. Of course. Stewardship is, ah, very much in my wheelhouse, he declared at the victory podium, perspiration glistening under the lights. A safe, steady course for our nation, a middle path between extremes! That is what Vespuria deserves. And what I, ah, intend. Yes. Intend.

Behind him, one could practically hear the rustling of permanent secretaries shuffling their briefing papers, ready to help him intend correctly for the next five years.

[b]Meanwhile in the House of Appointed[/b]

If the Stewards election had been anticlimax with bunting, the House of Appointed was its carnival sequel. A chamber of professional talkers, it had rapidly descended into what commentators politely described as [i]verbal jousting[/i] and what less charitable citizens simply called [i]a farce.[/i]

The Speaker bellowed Order! Order! so often that visitors assumed it was a religious chant. The benches roared with Hear, hear! at every conceivable syllable, regardless of meaning. Clapping was forbidden, which only meant members shouted louder to compensate.

[b]Mr. Speaker[/b]! cried a representative from the Southern bloc, rising to full height. It is intolerable that this government daresDARESto fund restoration of Hyperions ruins with the very same bonds that will leave my constituents destitute!

[i]Hear, hear![/i] came from his allies, though most of them had clearly not heard the speech beyond the word destitute.

Another leapt up from the opposition benches. Nonsense, sir, arrant nonsense! Those bonds will secure our financial future and restore our heritage, unlike the ruinous [i]policies[/i] of your party when last in office!

[i]Hear, hear![/i]

[b]Rubbish![/b] shouted another, thumping the bench.

[i]Withdraw! Withdraw![/i] roared yet another, finger stabbing the air like an enraged schoolteacher.

The Speaker thundered, Order! Ordaaaah! The Right Honourable Member will mind his tongue or find himself escorted from this chamber!

The Right Honourable Member in question sat down with the wounded dignity of a man who had been told his tie was the wrong color.

Into this chaos stepped Steward Hacker himself, papers clutched in his hands, expression halfway between determination and panic. He cleared his throat.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to present the governments economic program

About time! jeered a voice.

which is, ah, designed to increase GDP per capita bywell, by some percent, certainly, several of them

Specifics, man! Specifics! shouted an opposition backbencher, waving his order paper like a flag.

Yes, well, if the Honourable Member will allow me to finish, we shall be implementing a twelve-point plan. He fumbled the sheets. Or possibly thirteen, depending on how one counts the port modernization initiative, which, I must say, is quite robust

Laughter rippled across the benches.

Mr. Speaker, is the Steward proposing to govern the nation by arithmetic?

[i]Hear, hear![/i]

Better arithmetic than astrology! Hacker retorted, surprising even himself. A roar of approval erupted, half mocking, half genuine.

The Speaker pounded the gavel. Order! Order! This House will hear the Steward in silence!

Naturally, silence did not come. Instead, the chamber dissolved into the usual chorus of half-meant jeers, ironic cheers, and self-congratulatory applause disguised as vocal affirmation.

At length, the Steward slumped back to his bench, sweating but alive. The civil servants in the gallery exchanged knowing nods. He had survived. Just.

[b]Meanwhile in the House of Anointed[/b]

By contrast, the House of Anointed might as well have been in a different country. Here, decorum reigned supreme. Old men and good men, the odd old lady or good lady, new peers still adjusting to their unexpected coronets  all gathered in velvet silence to discuss the very same matters their counterparts had screamed over.

Baroness Emsworth, might I inquire whether the Hyperion bonds have safeguards for rural investors? asked an elderly Margrave, voice soft as parchment.

I believe so, Margrave, she replied gently. I have here a memorandum from the Treasury. Shall I read the relevant clause?

Yes, please. That would be most enlightening.

A clerk shuffled papers, spectacles glinting in the lamplight. The clause was read aloud. Nods circled the benches. Someone coughed. A quiet [i]Bless you[/i] followed, whispered in unison.

The Duke of Othmere raised his hand delicately. Might I suggest an amendment ensuring minority guild representation on the oversight board?

An excellent point, Duke, murmured the Countess beside him. Shall we submit that in writing, or would the Steward prefer it attached to the committee report?

Oh, attached, I think. Easier for the clerks.

And so the session continued: soft voices, careful amendments, actual questions asked and actually answered. It was, in its way, the most revolutionary part of the new Empire  a chamber where people behaved as if governance were serious business.

When the bells rang for adjournment, they rose, bowed, and filed out with dignity. Outside, the roar of the House of Appointed still echoed across the capital. Inside, the Anointed left behind nothing but neat papers and the faint smell of old ink.

[b]MILITARY-INDUSTRIAL CAMARADERIE[/b]

[b]The Knightless Army[/b]

The Vespurian Army was a patchwork quilt before unification, stitched together from three national traditions and a dozen regional variations. By rights it should have descended into confusion, infighting, or at least the polite sulking of rival general staffs. Instead, it produced something stranger: brotherhood at first sight.

Old guard veterans clinked cups in smoky officers clubs, laughing over tales of the war games that had once pitted them against each other. Young soldiers exchanged numbers with the enthusiasm of students at a summer festival, swapping insignias and patches as if they were collectible cards. The occasional queer kiss in the barracks drew nothing more than a cheer and another round of drinks.

Sergeants salivated openly at the recruitment prospects: suddenly, instead of three pools of conscripts, there was one enormous reservoir of eager, underemployed youth. Training camps swelled, drill squares rang with new accents, and paperwork flooded the quartermasters offices. A problem worth having, muttered one staff officer, staring down at requisition requests stacked higher than his helmet.

The true winners were the logicians and bean-counters, who thanked whichever god or pantheon they observed for the new colossal defense budget. Spreadsheets sang with fresh allocations: tanks ordered, artillery modernized, uniforms standardized. Even the medical corps cheered  they could finally afford proper prosthetics instead of the "temporary" solutions that had lingered for decades.

Special forces, of course, were hustled discreetly into the basement. No one wished to hear their comparative war crime stories over the campfire. Better to leave them muttering in their windowless training halls until such time as someone important required deniable results. BlackOps remained deeper still, in the kind of bureaucratic pit that even Satan might file a complaint about. Everyone agreed this was for the best.

And through it all, the Emperor himself performed the necessary pageantry: touring garrisons, shaking hands, penning letters of thanks to regimental headquarters, occasionally delivering solemn speeches that were more heartfelt than eloquent. Soldiers respected him for it. Civilians loved the photographs. Most importantly, pensions were solid, and everyone knew it.

[b]The Emperors Sailors[/b]

If the Army fused with a handshake, the Navy melded with a toast. Dockyards echoed with shanties in four dialects, all sung together with surprising harmony after the third round of rum. Sailors compared tattoos, ships compared tonnage, and admirals compared mustaches  all with an air of jovial competition rather than rancor.

The fleets meshed as if they had always been one. Coastal patrols dovetailed with deepwater squadrons, riverine flotillas linked with carrier groups, and suddenly the Vespurian banner fluttered across the straits with a confidence unseen in generations. Logistics officers nearly fainted with delight when they realized three incompatible supply chains could now be rationalized into one  a bureaucratic miracle that produced almost as much joy as new destroyers.

Of course, old rivalries flared now and then. A High Albic frigate crew might sneer at the Southern sailors seamanship, only to be humbled in gunnery trials. A coastal flotilla might boast of its speed, only to be overtaken by Highland-built cutters. But these contests rarely soured; instead, they became spectacles for spectatorship, with betting pools flourishing in dockside taverns.

Strategists toasted the Emperors sailors as the sharpest point of imperial projection. More than the Army or Air Arm, the Navy carried the image of a united Vespuria abroad  sleek hulls, new banners, and officers in uniforms that seemed designed to feature in recruitment posters. The sea was their domain, and now, their flag was one.

[b]The Military Myriad[/b]

The rest of the armed apparatus, sprawling and eclectic, took to unification with the same gusto. The Air Arm, always more expensive than sensible, exulted in expanded funding: new fighters, new bombers, new maintenance crews, and most importantly, new bases. Pilots strutted about in aviators, smug in the knowledge that their machines now dominated not one sky but three.

The magitech corps swelled into prominence, inheriting three different schools of arcane warfare and promptly declaring themselves indispensable. Engineers competed to see who could weld rune-engraved plating faster; artificers squabbled over whether Southern mana-conductors were superior to Highland crystal arrays. A new Ministry committee was hastily convened to prevent them from blowing up too many prototypes in the capital.

The intelligence services were, predictably, silent. Everyone assumed they were merging somewhere, somehow, into a hydra-headed entity of terrifying efficiency. Or inefficiency. No one knew, and no one dared to ask. BlackOps, for their part, had yet to acknowledge the empires existence at all. Everyone liked it that way.

And underpinning it all was money  rivers of it, surging from the treasury into armories, bases, and pensions. Soldiers smiled, sailors sang, airmen swaggered, engineers tinkered, and retirees cashed checks on time for once.

The Empire had many flaws, and many divisions yet to heal. But in the barracks and the dockyards, in the hangars and the workshops, one truth was undeniable: nothing united men and women so swiftly as a shared uniform, a bigger budget, and the promise that this time, their pensions would actually be paid.

[b]UNLIMITED POWER, LIMITED[/b]

[b]Humanity & Nonhumans[/b]

The new constitution startled many by extending legal protections across the spectrum of magical and nonhuman life. Elves, dwarves, bestials, and even the occasional undead citizen were guaranteed rights, pensions, and regulations. For the first time in centuries, a wood elf herbalist could register as a state-recognized alchemist, a dwarven rune-smith could qualify for industrial subsidies, and a revenant could technically qualify for a disability pension so long as they filled in Form 47-B (Posthumous Continuity of Benefits).

Reactions varied. The elves  especially the ancient ones who had been alive in the days of the Old Empire  treated it as both amusing and overdue. Some remarked that this was simply history repeating itself: men built institutions, men destroyed them, and then, centuries later, men rebuilt them with new acronyms. Dwarves cared less for the symbolism and more for the legal clarity; their guilds now had binding charters that even human courts recognized, which meant contracts were enforceable without sending a battalion to collect. Bestials, long caught between suspicion and novelty status, embraced the new protections with a wary optimism  employment protections, cultural rights, and even state-sponsored veterinary-magical healthcare made a difference.

Even the undead, often relegated to the margins, found themselves surprised to be acknowledged by law. Vampires muttered that they preferred not to be counted, but were quietly pleased their estates could now be inherited without centuries of legal wrangling. Liches, those relics of old eras, regarded the new statutes with dry contempt: to them, bureaucratic wards were as laughable as a sandcastle against the tide. Still, most complied  better to fill forms than face the Ministrys enforcement squads.

[b]Magic Resurgence[/b]

The greatest shock was not political but environmental. Across the land, ley-lines stirred, dormant nodes flared, and old wards groaned awake as if roused by the act of recognition itself. The bureaucrats called it residual arcane resurgence; the public called it magic being back.

For ordinary citizens, this meant the spectacular and the absurd. Weather mages were suddenly in demand to cool city heatwaves, potion-brewers found themselves selling elixirs alongside pharmacists, and fleshcrafters (under very strict supervision) were quietly contracted by hospitals to grow replacement organs. On the darker edges, there were reports of illicit curses, backyard necromancy, and a booming black market for unlicensed spellwork.

The Empires majority  practical, technological, and tax-paying  reacted with ambivalence. Many were thrilled by new conveniences: enchanted public transport, wards against burglary, even charm-assisted farming that boosted yields. But many more muttered at the cost. Magic meant licences, licences meant fees, and fees meant taxes. The revelation that one could now be fined for unregistered thaumaturgical activity provoked outrage in rural communities where low-level charms had been casual practice for generations. To the Ministry, it was governance. To the commoner, it was another bill.

The technological sector eyed the resurgence with suspicion but also opportunity. Hybrid magitech industries blossomed, blending spellcraft with circuitry, enchantments with turbines. Engineers joked that the real magic was making the Ministry approve their patents on time. Economists were blunter: magic had become a commodity, and commodities could be taxed.

[b]The Ministry[/b]

The grand merger of three Ministries of Magic into one was less a negotiation than an annexation, performed with wards, lawyers, and groaning filing cabinets. The new [i]Imperial Ministry of Thaumaturgy & Arcane Regulation[/i] was divided into departments with names long enough to require abbreviations: Licensing, Enforcement, Ward Management, Educational Oversight, Anti-Magical Security, Experimental Review, and the ever-dreaded Division of Prohibited Practices.

Schools of magic were standardized: every child with aptitude was to attend a registered institution, take exams, and graduate with a licence. The days of the wandering hedge-wizard were officially over, though many continued to operate until Enforcement caught them. Mandatory education meant a surge of demand for teachers, and suddenly retired sorcerers and half-forgotten mages were summoned from obscurity to lecture on proper rune-formation or potion ratios.

The Ministrys proudest achievement was the Ward Grid: a network of runic stones, inscribed and linked across the Empire, capable of registering the time and location of nearly all significant spellcasting. For the first time, a government could say with some confidence who had cast what, where, and when. It was, in theory, the great safeguard against abuse. In practice, it also became a lucrative fountain of fines, since forgetting to file a casting intent notice was an offense in itself.

Permits multiplied. To brew above Level III potions required certification; to summon elementals required not only a licence but also a liability insurance bond; necromancy was restricted to academic institutions and tightly supervised hospitals. Wards, fines, trials, and tribunals became as much a part of magical life as staves and runes.

Citizens sighed, cursed, and queued at the Ministry counters. And yet, for all the groaning, the truth was clear: magic was now a constitutional fact of the Empire. Not feared, not hidden, not merely tolerated  but institutionalized. Unlimited power, limited by parchment, signature, and seal.

[b]MINDBOGG-INDUSTRIAL COMPLEX[/b]

[b]Oh, We Survived?[/b]

The first miracle of unification was simply that the economy did not implode on day one. Instead, by some bureaucratic sleight of hand, three collapsing treasuries became one slightly more stable treasury. Customs houses were shuttered, their clerks reassigned to land registries and revenue services. Border tariffs  hated by merchants and adored by smugglers  were abolished overnight. The result was an instant 1520% surge in trade volumes, as goods that once sat marooned at checkpoints now flowed seamlessly across the Empire.

[b]Infrastructure:[/b] The Empire immediately turned its eyes to its bones: roads, rail, ports, and power. Five-year contracts were awarded to construction cartels tasked with doubling highway capacity on the north-south axes. Rail electrification projects began in earnest, with new locomotives jointly designed by industrial syndicates in High Albany and Hyperion. The government borrowed shamelessly on reconstruction bonds, but investors did not mind  every kilometre of track laid promised taxable commerce for a generation.

[b]Ports:[/b] Coastal cities were modernized to handle containerization and magitech shipping alike. Dredging projects deepened harbours for heavier cargoes, while customs operations were digitized  a shock to officials used to stamping parchment but a boon to exporters who cut clearance times from weeks to hours.

[b]Energy:[/b] A patchwork of coal, hydro, geothermal, and experimental magitech reactors was consolidated into a single Imperial Grid. The cost was staggering but the returns obvious: energy costs for industry fell by 18% within two years. Cheap power lured heavy industries home and gave small manufacturers the margins to expand.

[b]Housing & Urban Works:[/b] Hyperion City  once a tent city amid ruins  became the showcase. Entire districts were rebuilt under Heritage Redevelopment Contracts, which forced corporations to use local labour, preserve key sites, and publish transparent budgets. The housing stock was expanded by 120,000 units in the first wave, stabilizing rents and preventing riotous overcrowding. Construction unions became the most powerful civic players in the city, their banners waving proudly beside Imperial heraldry.

And for once, the numbers actually added up.

[b]No Cynade, Darling, Just Coffee.[/b]

The corporate elite, long fractious, discovered a taste for collusion disguised as patriotism. The Ministry of Finance coaxed them into syndicates: sectoral councils where rival firms now pooled research budgets, shared patents, and synchronized production schedules. Competition is foreign, cooperation is domestic became the unspoken motto.

[b]Industrial Cartels:[/b]

[i]Automotives[/i]  rival manufacturers jointly developed electric-magitech hybrid engines. Instead of undercutting each other, they divided markets by region and class, ensuring stable profits.

[i]Petro-energy conglomerates[/i]  once at each others throats, they merged downstream operations and diverted capital into renewables, hedging their survival by owning both the oil rig and the wind farm.

[i]Steel & Heavy Industry[/i]  consolidated into a national trust, supplying both civilian industry and the rapidly expanding military machine.

[b]Food Security:[/b] An Imperial Food Trust pooled agribusiness logistics, ensuring that surplus wheat from hinterlands reached urban bakeries without spoilage. Modernized silos, refrigerated transport, and subsidies for mechanized farming cut costs by 23% while stabilizing bread prices  a political godsend in a country that once rioted over grain.

[b]Finance:[/b] The Imperial Bank introduced a dual-credit system: industrial bonds for corporations and microcredit schemes for small business. Both were guaranteed by the state, reducing risk and drawing private lenders into ventures they would otherwise avoid. The quiet genius was that repayments were indexed to output, not arbitrary schedules, aligning debt service with actual production.

[b]Labour Policy:[/b] Apprenticeship programs exploded. Every major industrial project was required to accept a ratio of apprentices to masters. Tens of thousands of young Vespurians entered paid training in construction, logistics, magitech maintenance, and port operations. Unlike the Old Empires gilded academies, this was training for employment, not prestige.

Unemployment plummeted. By the end of year three, every major industrial city boasted labour participation rates above 70%. The unions  legal, loud, and occasionally rowdy  were tied into corporatist councils. Strikes were not outlawed but ritualized: grievances were aired, arbitrated, and settled before production lines froze. The state quietly subsidized wage floors to keep peace, but called it productivity bonuses.

[b]Loyal Labourers of the Lux Dynasty[/b]

The people themselves became the engine. The universal pension system, once theoretical, became real  every citizen contributing and every retiree guaranteed. Health care followed, partially funded by a levy on corporations, partially from general taxation. Workers now lived long enough to claim their pensions, and pensions ensured loyalty to the Lux Dynasty.

[b]Urban Development & Employment:[/b] Old industrial sites were rehabilitated rather than abandoned. Defunct factories were converted into modular industrial parks, where SMEs could lease floor space with shared utilities. This reduced capital barriers for small entrepreneurs and gave cities new economic lifeblood. Hyperion became the flagship  a hybrid of restored marble ruins and glass industrial blocks, where welders and curators worked side by side.

[b]Circular Industrial Planning:[/b] Nothing went to waste. Mining output fed steel mills. Steel mills supplied rail. Rail carried timber. Timber fed shipyards. Shipyards demanded magitech engines. Engines required arcane stabilizers, which created demand for trained magi, which justified schools, which fed the education budget. For once, the loop closed.

[b]International Trade:[/b] Elseyr and other neighbours became markets rather than enemies. Export credit facilities backed Vespurian firms entering risky foreign contracts. State-backed insurance minimized defaults. Ports were granted preferential slots to Vespurian shippers. Slowly, the Empires economy entwined with its neighbours, binding them in dependency.

[b]The Cultural Economy:[/b] Not to be forgotten, the Age of Heroes industry continued pumping revenue. Streaming platforms, VR reenactments, heritage tourism, and merchandise all generated foreign exchange. Archaeology was monetized. Festivals were licensed. Historical destruction simulators, bizarrely enough, outsold every strategy game abroad. Economists stopped complaining when tax revenue rolled in.

And through it all, the branding never faltered. Each payslip was stamped with the phrase: For Service, For Empire, For Lux. Workers rolled their eyes, cashed the slip, and went back to work. Cynicism and loyalty coexisted, as they always had.

[b]MEANWHILE, THE LUXS...[/b]

[b]Gaudy Couple[/b]

"...I look ridiculous." The Emperor said.

"Nonsense, besides it's the most modern thing the court would let you wear casually." The Empress said, gesturing at her husband for almost three decades on the giant, frankly absurdly gilded no, actually made of gold, mirror.

"Gaudy then." He flicked the cape. And again. And again.

"Stop that." She said, swatting his hand, "You're not Batman."

"I'm a Superman fan." The Emperor frowned again, "At least you look good."

"I always look good, besides I've always been up to fashion, who do you think organised the colour scheme of your suits during your political campaigns?" She relied whilst taking a look at herself in the mirror.

"...my suits were organised?" The Emperor asked with a confused frown as he crossed his eyes, until his wife flicked his forehead.

"How did you ever pass a degree in law?" She muttered.

"Being as smart as I am funny." The Emperor said, adjusting his suit-thing.

"Hmn." The Empress hummed back as she left for the door, but the guards outside opened it for her before she could, earning a frown.

The Emperor quickly followed after her, not without waving at the guards who just saluted.

"Do you think they'll finish installing elevators or...let us use carts around this place? It's humongous." The Emperor said.

"Of course it is, it's the size of a small city. It'll be good for your cardio, you know?" She told them as they walked.

"Good for my cardio? Dear, we're almost half a century old, I don't want to waste a decade getting from my bedroom to my office to the dining hall." The Emperor frowned ahead at the, in his opinion, gaudy imperial dynastic architecture.

"You can always get a court mage to teleport you." She replied nonplussed.

He grimaced, "Ugh. No. I'll take walking with my bowels undisturbed." He replied, "So, have you heard what happened a bit to the East?"

"Ah yes, some friends in the military texted me about it. Revolution and barbarism." The Empress said, sneering at the mere thought.

"They were being quite mistreated." The Emperor added as they walked.

"Tsk. No excuse. From the people. From the royals. From everyone. Natural selection, I say." The Emperor replied sternly.

"Dear, please." The Emperor sighed, "Besides...I do agree on the barbaric side, vengeance is not justice. They've gone to our Elseyr half, you know?" He commented to her 

"Hmn. So the Crowned Stag has welcomed the Exiles. Good for them, I suppose. I almost expected them to become pirates." The Empress replied, "Why? Feeling jealous they didn't go to you?" She smiled at him as they began descending some large stairs.

"Not particularly, I'm rather worried for them. I was thinking of inviting them over, loaning them a home they can...sleep and rest their weary hearts and minds from all this revolutionary issues." The Emperor supplied as he linked arms with her, a few guards by the stairs saluted them, he nodded back.

"Well, it's not like I care. Should I call the children to the Capital then?" The Empress asked, holding onto his arm.

"Yes, that would be rather nice. I'll write to Jim." The Emperor nodded.

"At least I won't have to slave over the oven this time, and do try to bother sounding eloquent, I don't know, use Grammarly on your phone then pen the thing. You got secretaries too, you know?" The Empress said.

"I'll be bones and dust before I bloody well let anyone but you see my downright abominable letter sketches, and God Bless Autocorrect." The Emperor chuckled dryly, "...how long to the gardens?" He asked.

"Just a few blocks more." She replied and the Emperor made an undignified noise.

[b]Invitation[/b]

Jim stared at the letter.

Then at Humphrey.

Then at the letter.

"... where's Fleuschia?"

Humphrey smiled, "If I may, Imperial Steward, they're a bit to the west of us last the central sea." The civil servant supplied, not correcting the misspellings.

"Perhaps...it may be prudent to let Bernard write the letter, it's a small matter that I'm sure the Emperor can handle with the Imperial Court, no need to busy yourself, you've got many state visits after all." Humphrey added.
